notes:
# Proverbs 26: verse-by-verse research notes

**Sources and gaps.** I read David Guzik's Enduring Word chapter, Wesley's Notes, the Pulpit Commentary (on StudyLight) and the Bible Hub/StudyLight pages, which include Gill, Ellicott, Barnes, Benson, Poole, Matthew Henry and the NET notes. I didn't reach any pages on the Lutheran, Pentecostal-denominational, Catholic/Orthodox or bibleodyssey.org sites. The Catholic material below comes only from translations and from the Pulpit Commentary's comments on the Vulgate and Jerome. The online copy of Guzik's commentary I read was cut off at verse 18, so his notes on verses 20–28 come from the page's summary and search excerpts. On these pages the Protestant traditions mostly agree. Verse 10 has a real disagreement, but it's about translation, not denomination.

---

**v. 1** — Snow in summer and rain at harvest are out of place and ruin the grain crop. Honour given to a fool is just as out of place and can be just as harmful (Guzik, citing Waltke). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-26/
- The Pulpit Commentary says a harvest storm seemed almost unnatural (1 Sam 12:17). Honouring a fool only confirms him in his folly and gives him more power to do harm. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-26.html
- Matthew Henry applies it to rulers who promote bad men, who then misuse their power. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_026.cfm

**v. 2** — Main reading: an undeserved curse has no magical power. It needs a real cause before God (Guzik, citing Waltke and Kidner on Balaam, Num 23:8). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-26/
- Wesley: the innocent person escapes the curse the way a bird escapes the fowler. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/proverbs-26.html
- **Textual question.** The MT has the negative ("will not come"), but some commentators follow the Qere reading, meaning an undeserved curse will come back to the one who gave it. The NET note adds that there is no referent for the suffix, making it syntactically difficult. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=pro&chapter=26&verse=2
- Barnes links the alternative reading to the English proverb, "Curses, like young chickens, always come home to roost." The Pulpit Commentary rejects it, though it seems to have been used by St. Jerome. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/26-2.htm
- **Against superstition** (NET note): the ancient world commonly believed blessings and curses had power in themselves, but scripture makes it clear that the power of a blessing or a curse depends on the power of the one behind it. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=pro&chapter=26&verse=2
- **Protestant polemic.** Gill uses the verse against Rome: "what are all the anathemas of the church of Rome? who can curse whom God has not cursed?" https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/26-2.htm
- **Catholic translation.** The Douay-Rheims follows the other reading: "so a curse uttered without cause shall come upon a man." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/proverbs-26.html
- **Popular "spiritual law" reading.** Everett's Study Notes says not a single curse comes without a cause; if the basis exists in a person's life, it can be removed and God's blessings will come in its place. It ties this to seedtime and harvest as a basic law. The page doesn't name a movement, and I couldn't confirm which tradition it belongs to. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/proverbs-26.html

**v. 3** — Fools who won't learn from wise words have to learn through pain (Guzik). Kidner notes the proverb speaks to us both as people dealing with fools and as possible fools ourselves. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-26/
- Pulpit: in early times horses were driven, not ridden. The Septuagint reads "a rod for a lawless nation." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-26.html

**vv. 4–5** — Every tradition I read explains the apparent contradiction the same way.
- Benson: easily reconciled, by considering the difference of persons, times, places, and other circumstances, and of the manner of answering. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/26-4.htm
- Barnes: verse 4 means trading insults on the fool's level. Verse 5 means saying the right word at the right time to expose his error (same page).
- Wesley (Methodist): verse 4 forbids copying the fool with angry or insulting words. Verse 5 calls for sharp reproof that shows him up and shames him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/proverbs-26.html
- Gill gives examples of answering nothing: Hezekiah's men before Rabshakeh, and Christ before the Pharisees. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/26-4.htm
- Guzik says verse 5 is for when it will do good or is needed for God's glory (citing Poole). He adds Ross's point that life's problems can't always be solved by one rule. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-26/
- Pulpit cites Jesus' answers that turned trick questions aside (Matt 21:23; 22:21). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-26.html

**v. 6** — Sending a fool with a message is like hurting yourself (Guzik). He notes that God chooses the "foolish things" (1 Cor 1:27) but wants them to be more than fools. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-26/
- Wesley: it's like sending a man with no legs. In Scripture, "drinking" often means receiving something in full. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/proverbs-26.html

**v. 7** — Wisdom in a fool's mouth is useless (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-26/
- Matthew Henry: the verse fits the man who talks religion but lives a wicked life. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_026.cfm
- Pulpit discusses the hard Hebrew word. It notes Luther read it as "dancing" and argues for "hang loose." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-26.html

**v. 8** — A stone tied into a sling can't be thrown and may swing back and hit the slinger (Waltke and Garrett, in Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-26/
- Pulpit: the Revised Version margin reads "bag of gems in a heap of stones," which Pulpit rejects. The Vulgate reads a "heap of Mercury," which Pulpit calls an anachronism. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-26.html

**v. 9** — Trapp (in Guzik) applies it to ungodly people who twist Scripture and harm themselves and others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-26/
- Pulpit: the picture is a drunk man waving a thornbush around, not one who fails to feel a thorn. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-26.html

**v. 10** — This is the chapter's biggest disagreement, and it's about translation.
- **"God" reading (KJV/NKJV):** Gill, Wesley and the Geneva notes take it to mean God pays every sinner what he deserves. Wesley says this applies whether they sinned in ignorance or on purpose. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/proverbs-26.html
- **Rejection of that reading:** Barnes: the word "God" is not in the original… The simplest and best interpretation is: As the archer that woundeth everyone, so is he who hireth the fool. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/26-10.htm
- Pulpit lists many renderings and thinks the Hebrew text may be damaged. It says the passage has given greater difficulty than almost any other (same page).
- **Catholic translation:** The Douay-Rheims has "Judgment determineth causes: and he that putteth a fool to silence, appeaseth anger." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/proverbs/26-10.html

**v. 11** — A fool won't change without a dramatic transformation (Guzik). 2 Peter 2:22 uses this verse for a sinner going back to sin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-26/
- Henry: sinners who have been convinced only and not converted, return to sin again. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_026.cfm
- Pulpit speaks of "partial repentance." The Septuagint adds a line also found in Sirach 4:21. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-26.html
- I didn't find a page that debates this verse in terms of whether believers can lose their salvation.

**v. 12** — The man who is "wise in his own eyes" will never learn (Guzik). Morgan's test: when we stop seeking God's guidance, we are wise in our own conceit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-26/
- Pulpit compares him to the self-righteous Pharisee (Luke 18:14) and quotes Chrysostom: it is better to be a fool than haughty. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-26.html

**v. 13** — The lazy man is creative, but only at making excuses (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-26/
- Henry: the excuse covers religion as well as work. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_026.cfm

**v. 14** — A door moves but goes nowhere (Ross, in Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-26/
- Wesley says the same. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/proverbs-26.html

**v. 15** — Henry calls it a deliberate exaggeration that shows how the sin punishes itself. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_026.cfm

**v. 16** — Seven means completeness (Clarke and Pulpit). Kidner notes the lazy man never sees himself in these verses. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-26/
- Henry: conceit and laziness feed each other. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_026.cfm

**v. 17** — Grabbing a dog's ears is hard to keep up and dangerous to stop. Guzik notes Jesus refused to step into another man's dispute (Luke 12:14). Bridges: suffering as a Christian is different from suffering as a busybody. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-26/

**vv. 18–19** — Henry: the deceiver is a "madman." Saying "I was joking" doesn't excuse him, but people shouldn't be unable to take a joke either. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_026.cfm
- Guzik links these verses to James 3. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-3/

**vv. 20–22** — Gossip is fuel for strife. Gossip also shapes what we think of people before we've checked it. Guzik adds that the listener is as guilty as the teller. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-26/
- Henry: gossips should be removed from families and churches. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_026.cfm

**v. 23** — Like cheap silver coating on clay: attractive outside, worthless inside (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-26/
- Wesley: "burning" means burning with malice. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/proverbs-26.html

**vv. 24–26** — The secret hater fools himself as well as others and should not be trusted (Guzik). God will expose him in the end. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-26/
- Wesley on v. 26: "deceit" means pretending to love. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/proverbs-26.html

**v. 27** — Wesley: the man rolls a stone uphill meaning to hurt someone, and it comes back on him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/proverbs-26.html
- Pulpit links this justice to verse 2. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-26.html

**v. 28** — The liar actually hates his victims. Flattery builds up pride and ruins people (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-26/
